name: Frequency specific microcurrent

lead: Frequency specific microcurrent (FSM) delivers very small electrical currents, in the microampere range, in specific pairs of frequencies through electrodes, graphite gloves or moistened towels placed on the skin. Practitioners use it for pain, tissue tension and recovery, and some people connect it with facial microcurrent toning, which is a related but different cosmetic use.

For looks, the proposed routes are indirect: faster recovery from training soreness could support more consistent exercise, and tissue-softening claims are sometimes discussed alongside face and neck tension. Published research includes small randomized trials on muscle soreness and stress and several case reports.

paras: FSM is typically delivered in a clinic by a trained practitioner, who selects frequency pairs for a target condition and applies them for a set time, often in a series of visits. Consumer microcurrent facial devices are separate products, usually used at home with a conductive gel.
The microcurrent range used is below the level of sensation and published case reports describe it as safe and non-painful. Evidence is limited and mostly from small studies.

angle.text: For looks, FSM is discussed as a way to speed recovery between training sessions and to relieve tissue tension, which people connect with consistent training and a relaxed appearance. A related cosmetic microcurrent use, facial toning, is a separate application.

lead: Frequency specific microcurrent (FSM) is an electrotherapy technique that applies low-amperage currents in specific paired frequencies to the skin, with the aim of treating pain, inflammation and tissue tension.[1][2] Its modern form is credited to chiropractor Carolyn McMakin, who in 1995 paired frequency lists from the 1920s with modern microcurrent devices.[1]

In looksmaxxing and skin-care discussions, FSM appears next to microcurrent as a category: low-level current devices marketed for facial toning and muscle recovery. People interested in appearance mention it for post-workout recovery and for tissue softening, a palpable change practitioners say they observe within seconds of application.[3][4]
Published research includes a randomized trial in delayed onset muscle soreness, pilot trials in scleroderma and in stress, retrospective data in neck and back pain, and case reports.[5][6][7][8]

paras: FSM sends pairs of frequencies of microampere-level current to chosen places on the skin using conductive graphite gloves, moistened towels or gel patches; practitioners report palpable tissue softening and warming within seconds of applying frequencies chosen for a condition.[3] Microcurrent therapy in general uses currents under one milliampere, below the roughly one-milliamp level of TENS, and has a history going back to experiments in the 1800s.[9]

Early twentieth-century physicians in the US, UK and Germany explored frequency-based electrical therapies, among them Albert Abrams and his frequency lists, which fell out of favor in the 1930s.[1] In 1995 McMakin paired a list of frequencies from the 1920s with modern microcurrent devices, treated fibromyalgia and myofascial pain patients, and published a 2010 textbook on FSM in pain management.[1]

Proponents describe resonance of tissues with matched frequencies and increased cellular ATP production in vitro; the 2013 paper on tissue softening proposes a connection to muscle tone, citing Irvin Korr's gamma-loop hypothesis.[1][3] Authors of the cited literature note that mechanisms are not well established.[9]

A 2022 study examined self-rated recovery and mood after resistance training with muscle microcurrent application.[4] Facial microcurrent toning devices are sold by cosmetic companies; the general Wikipedia article on microcurrent notes this use and cites company sources.[9]

In a randomized sham-controlled trial of 35 healthy adults, FSM on one leg after eccentric exercise was associated with lower soreness scores than the untreated leg at 24, 48 and 72 hours.[5] Two pilot studies in 17 scleroderma patients reported improved hand function and Raynaud's symptoms.[6] A 2025 pilot randomized trial in adults with distress reported fewer somatic symptoms in the FSM group than in relaxation alone at the first assessment.[7] A retrospective case-control study examined FSM as an adjunct in neck and low back pain, and case reports cover wounded warriors and a child with torticollis.[8][10][2] No studies found have tested FSM for facial appearance.
